Title: SEC asks investment firms to prove they have access to shares in startups
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The Securities and Exchange Commission has stepped up its examinations of firms behind so-called special purpose vehicles (SPVs) that claim to offer exposure to private company investments, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday, citing people familiar with the matter.
The SEC has been asking registered investment advisers for proof that their SPVs own or have exposure to the shares in private companies that they claim to, the Journal said.
Reuters could not immediately verify the report.

Title: 'Please hold on': Wife's plea for missing firefighter in Nepal
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: "Assalamualaikum, my husband. Where are you? Please hold on. Our family misses you so much."
That was the heartbreaking plea from a woman known as @azielashaharuddin on Threads, whose husband, senior Fire and Rescue Department officer Mohd Sani Harul, remains missing following the devastating floods in Nepal last Wednesday.
Posting a photo of herself with Sani in front of the Kaaba in Makkah, she said the family had received no word from him or his team for the past five days.
"Our family is filled with hope, longing and fear. We are still waiting for news, but until now, we do not know where he is or how he is doing," she wrote today.
Mohd Sani and another Malaysian Fire and Rescue Department officer, Mohd Fakhrul Munir Mohd Isa, are among 56 Malaysians who remain uncontactable following the devastating floods in Nepal's Rasuwa district.
Fire and Rescue Department director-general Datuk Seri Hisham Mohamad earlier said that the two officers, including Sani, who is deputy director of the Planning and Research Division at the department's headquarters, were in Nepal for a trekking expedition to Everest Base Camp.
He said they were initially scheduled to depart for Nepal on Aug 22, but their trip was rescheduled due to a clash with another programme.
In her post, @azielashaharuddin also prayed that her husband would continue to hold on and return safely and in good health to his family.
"Bring him back to his children and relatives who are waiting for him. Bring him home safely and in good health.
"If he is fighting to survive, strengthen him. Give him patience and hope, and remind him that help is always near," she wrote.
She said the family would continue waiting for Sani's return and hoping he would make it safely back to Malaysia.
"Do not let fear overcome us.
"Give us the patience to keep waiting and the strength to keep trying. You know how much we miss him and how much we long to see his face again.
"We want to embrace him again. There may be words we have yet to say to him and things we still hope to have the chance to do together.
"If there is still a chance for us to meet him again, let that meeting happen. Let us see his face and hear his voice again.
"Let us embrace him again and give our family a chance to be grateful for his safe return," she wrote.

Title: Traders put strategy first
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's fast-expanding online trading community is increasingly choosing trading platforms based on strategy, market exposure and the flexibility needed to navigate rapidly changing market conditions, rather than simply on which system offers the most features.
That is among the key findings of a 2026 trading platform guide released by JustMarkets, which suggests that the long-running debate over MetaTrader 4 (MT4) and MetaTrader 5 (MT5) is less about identifying a technological winner and more about matching the right tools to individual trading habits and strategies.
The guide said traders typically select platforms based on their experience, preferred trading style and the range of instruments they trade. While some remain with familiar systems that suit their established routines, others move to more advanced platforms as their strategies become increasingly complex and their market needs evolve.
"Traders often ask us which platform is 'better', but in practice the platform that works best is the one that aligns with your specific trading strategy and daily habits," JustMarkets said in a statement.
MT4 retains its pull for forex-focused traders, delivering a lean, familiar environment. Its lightweight build, speed, and ease of use suit those running well-defined strategies or favouring a streamlined setup without overloaded analytics.
MT5, meanwhile, is increasingly being used by traders seeking access to a wider range of financial instruments and more sophisticated analytical tools.
Behavioural shifts are also driving investors away from relying on a single platform.
"In today's fast-paced markets, flexibility is important. We see a growing number of clients using the analytical depth of MT5 alongside the browser-based access of our Web Terminal," the company said in a statement.
JustMarkets said that the pattern mirrors a wider evolution: traders are matching platforms to market conditions, strategy, and analytical need. Mobile and web-based access are gaining ground as traders seek market access untethered to a desktop.
For CFD traders, MT4 and MT5 remain workhorses for analysis and execution, while web solutions such as the JustMarkets Web Terminal offer instant, installation-free access.
The company casts the debate not as a winner-takes-all contest, but as a workflow choice: MT4 brings simplicity and efficiency; MT5 delivers breadth and flexibility.
"The real decision is not about choosing one platform over the other but about understanding how each tool may fit into a trading workflow and how additional solutions like web-based entry may improve flexibility and responsiveness in real market conditions."

Title: Economics of shared production
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The recent debate over whether Penang historically "belongs" to Kedah illustrates how easily discussions of federalism can conflate fundamentally different questions.
History explains how political relationships evolved. Constitutions determine legal authority. Fiscal arrangements determine how revenues and responsibilities are divided. Economic geography tells us something else: how investment, labour, production and supply chains actually function.
Confusing these questions risks turning legitimate historical discussion into unnecessary economic competition.
For Malaysia, the distinction matters because economic activity increasingly crosses state boundaries even when political institutions do not. Penang and Kedah are a good example.
Penang possesses one of Malaysia's most mature electrical and electronics ecosystems, built over five decades around multinational investment, engineering talent and supplier networks. But Northern Malaysia's manufacturing ecosystem no longer ends at Penang's border.
Kulim has become an important extension of that production geography. Penang and Kulim are now recognised as key Malaysian hubs for semiconductor manufacturing, wafer fabrication, advanced packaging and technology-intensive industry.
The implication is straightforward: Penang and Kedah are constitutionally separate states, but important parts of their economies increasingly function as one production system.
Penang contributes mature industrial networks, connectivity, suppliers and a global manufacturing brand. Kedah contributes industrial land, expanding high-technology capacity and room for scale. Their advantage increasingly lies in the combination.
The more useful policy question is therefore not which state possesses the stronger historical claim. It is whether both states can create more economic value together than separately.
The Economy Has Already Crossed the Boundary
Malaysia still conducts much economic planning through administrative jurisdictions. Investment statistics are reported by state. Industrial parks sit within state boundaries.
Infrastructure projects are often justified locally, while political credit is claimed state by state. Production networks behave differently.
A semiconductor company does not organise its supply chain according to constitutional boundaries. Engineers may live in one state and work in another. Suppliers may operate across several industrial zones. Components may be manufactured in Kedah, tested or packaged elsewhere, transported through Penang and exported through global logistics networks.
Trade data illustrate how externally connected both economies already are. DOSM reported a trade openness index of 575.1 for Penang and 234.2 for Kedah in 2024. Penang also remained Malaysia's largest exporting state in 2025.
Yet Malaysia devotes far more attention to measuring trade with China, the United States, Singapore or Europe than to understanding how value moves between Penang, Kedah, Perak and other Malaysian regions.
That is a statistical blind spot.
We know a great deal about Malaysia's external integration. We know considerably less about its internal production integration.
From State Competition to Regional Competitiveness
Federalism inevitably produces competition between states. That can be healthy when it encourages better infrastructure, faster approvals and stronger investment promotion. It becomes inefficient when neighbouring states treat complementary assets as mutually exclusive.
Penang does not have to become Kedah. Kedah does not have to become Penang.
Penang's scarcity of industrial land can be complemented by Kedah's capacity for expansion. Kedah's industrial growth can benefit from Penang's supplier networks, global reputation, technical workforce and connectivity.
The objective should not be to replicate one state in the other. It should be to create a regional production architecture in which each specialises according to comparative advantage while benefiting from the capabilities of its neighbour.
That is the difference between state competition and regional competitiveness.
The first asks: Which state won the investment?
The second asks: How much value can Northern Malaysia capture from it?
That is a far more useful question.
A Northern Production Strategy
Malaysia should increasingly treat the Penang-Kedah industrial corridor as a functional economic region.
This requires no alteration to constitutional boundaries or state authority. It requires coordination.
A Northern Regional Production Council could bring together the Federal Government, Penang and Kedah, with Perak and Perlis participating where relevant. Its mandate should be economic: industrial land, supply chains, transport, water, energy, logistics, skills and research infrastructure.
Talent should be among its first priorities.
A semiconductor ecosystem cannot be divided neatly along state lines when companies compete for the same engineers, technicians and graduates. Skills planning should therefore respond to the needs of the regional cluster, not merely separate administrative jurisdictions.
The same applies to infrastructure. Roads, railways, water, power and logistics networks generate benefits that cross state borders.
Malaysia also needs better data.
DOSM's national Input-Output tables already show how goods and services flow between industries and how producers depend upon one another. The next step should be stronger regional and interregional analysis.
Policymakers should know how much manufacturing output in Kedah depends upon services and inputs originating in Penang; how much value generated in Penang relies upon suppliers in Kedah or Perak; and whether a new semiconductor investment produces its largest multiplier in the host state or across the wider northern economy.
Regional Input-Output tables could distinguish between the location of production and the geography of economic benefit.
Without that information, states will continue competing over headline investment numbers without understanding where the resulting value actually flows.
Strong States, Strong Regions
None of this requires weakening state identity. Strong state institutions should make cooperation easier, not harder.
Penang's success need not come at Kedah's expense. Kedah's industrial expansion need not diminish Penang. A stronger Kulim can deepen the northern semiconductor ecosystem; a stronger Penang can provide the networks, capabilities and connectivity that amplify Kedah's growth.
The principle extends beyond the north.
Johor and Negeri Sembilan can cooperate around manufacturing and logistics. Selangor, Kuala Lumpur and Negeri Sembilan already form overlapping labour and housing markets. Perak can connect more deeply to the northern E&E corridor.
Malaysia's economic geography is becoming regional even while much of its governance remains state-based.
That gap must narrow.
The Penang-Kedah debate therefore offers a larger lesson for Malaysian federalism.
History should be understood. Constitutional arrangements should be respected. But neither should prevent economic cooperation where geography, production and shared prosperity make it rational.
The most important boundary in Malaysia's next phase of development may not be the one between Penang and Kedah.
It may be the boundary between an old model of competing states and a new model of cooperating regional economies.

Title: Kelantan sultanate crown: an ageless local craftsman's creation
Article:
KOTA BARU: Unlike most states, which once commissioned their royal crowns from England, the Kelantan Sultanate has a unique distinction — its royal crown was crafted by a local Malay artisan believed to have originated from Kampung Kubang Pasu here.
The more than 100-year-old crown is being displayed to the public for the first time at the Kelantan Heritage Weapons Festival 2026 at Istana Balai Besar here, which runs from Aug 16 to Sept 5.
Kelantan Sultan's Office Protocol Officer Mohamed Safaruddin Ismail said the idea for the crown was conceived by Sultan Ismail ibni Almarhum Sultan Muhammad IV, who ruled Kelantan from 1920 to 1944, and it was first used during his coronation ceremony on April 28, 1921.
At the ceremony, Tengku Temenggung Abdul Ghaffar ibni Almarhum Sultan Muhammad II placed the crown on Sultan Ismail, making it part of the history of the Kelantan Sultanate.
"The uniqueness of this crown lies in the fact that while most states had their royal crowns made in England, Kelantan's crown was crafted by a Kelantanese Malay artisan believed to have come from Kampung Kubang Pasu," he told Bernama recently.
Mohamed Safaruddin said the crown demonstrates the goldsmithing skills of the local community at the time, which were capable of producing a royal regalia of such high artistic value.
He said the crown was originally made from 16 ten-carat gold nuggets and featured carvings of young dala leaf motifs, as well as a crescent and five-pointed star at the top, set against royal blue velvet.
"During the reign of Almarhum Sultan Yahya Petra ibni Almarhum Sultan Ibrahim, 470 diamonds and 52 emeralds and rubies were added, while a further 721 diamonds and 44 emeralds were added during the reign of Almarhum Sultan Ismail Petra ibni Almarhum Sultan Yahya Petra," he said.
The crown is also adorned with ermine, or stoat, fur, whose white winter coat was historically associated with luxury in royal attire.
"This is the only crown of the Kelantan Sultanate and is usually brought out only to be placed to the right of the throne during the Sultan's Birthday celebrations, so not everyone has the opportunity to see it up close," he said.
Mohamed Safaruddin said the crown was chosen as the festival's main attraction following public interest in previous exhibitions of Kelantan royal regalia, including the Tok Chu keris with the Sampir Kuseriwa in 2024 and the royal tribute artefact Bunga Emas last year.
He said the stand for the crown is made of 999 pure gold and weighs almost one kilogram, while its actual value has not been disclosed for security reasons.
"Throughout the festival, strict security measures are in place involving public security personnel, while the crown is kept in a special palace vault," he said.
The festival also features traditional weapons, pitis coins and other Kelantan heritage treasures.
Organisers are targeting 50,000 visitors, compared with 42,000 last year, with direct Jakarta-Kota Bharu flights also expected to attract more foreign tourists, particularly Indonesians. — BERNAMA

Title: Local institutions extend buying streak to five weeks with RM200.5mil inflow
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Local institutions extended their net buying streak on Bursa Malaysia to five consecutive weeks, recording net inflows of RM200.5 million last week, MBSB Investment Bank Bhd (MBSB IB) said.
In its weekly Fund Flow Report for the week ended Aug 28, 2026, the investment bank said average daily trading volume saw a broad-based increase; retailers were up by 11.6 per cent, local institutions by 14.3 per cent, and foreign institutions by 96.5 per cent.
"Meanwhile, the retailers reverted to net buying after a week of net selling, recording RM165.5 million in net inflows compared with lower net outflows of RM42.0 million in the prior week," it said.
It said foreign institutions extended their net selling streak to four consecutive weeks on Bursa Malaysia, recording RM366.0 million in net outflows last week.
"This came during a shortened trading week, with the market closed on Tuesday in conjunction with the Birthday of Prophet Muhammad.
"Only Wednesday recorded net foreign inflows of RM94.4 million; meanwhile, the largest net outflows were recorded on Friday (-RM238.7 million), followed by Thursday (-RM140.5 million) and Monday (-RM81.1 million)," it said.
MBSB IB said the top three sectors to record net inflows from foreign institutions were transportation and logistics (RM129.5 million), healthcare (RM74.0 million) and property (RM32.0 million).
Meanwhile, it said the top three sectors to record net foreign outflows were financial services (-RM245.5 million), construction (-RM92.4 million) and telecommunications and media (-RM86.3 million).
Across the eight Asian markets MBSB IB monitors, foreign investors extended their net selling streak to two consecutive weeks, recording US$1.68 billion in net outflows last week, the bank said.
Net outflows were led mainly by South Korea, followed by Thailand, the Philippines and Malaysia; meanwhile, Taiwan, India, Vietnam and Indonesia were the only markets to record net foreign inflows, though these were insufficient to offset the region's overall net selling, it said.

Title: AI data centres could double urban heat island effect
Article:
Sharmini_NST:
slug HEATISLAND (from BH print)
KUALA LUMPUR: Aggressive, large-scale development of artificial intelligence (AI) data centres could double the urban heat island effect, with heat potentially spreading up to 10km from the facilities, a new study has found.
According to recent foreign research by several international universities, including the University of Cambridge and Nanyang Technological University, large-scale data centres create heat islands, with ground surface temperatures in surrounding areas rising by about two degrees Celsius once operations begin.
Sahabat Alam Malaysia (SAM) president Meenakshi Raman said heat risks can occur even before data centre operations begin, as soon as forested areas are cleared for construction.
"The loss of forests, which serve as natural carbon sinks and help regulate surrounding temperatures, will indirectly cause localised temperature increases. This means forest loss alone, even before a data centre is built, is enough to elevate heat levels in the surrounding area," she said.
"Given that the nation's energy supply is mostly generated by fossil fuels, these data centres could become major sources of carbon emissions for the country. Consequently, this could run counter to Malaysia's international commitments under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)," she told Berita Harian.
She said Malaysia has yet to demonstrate that large-scale AI data centre developments fully account for risks related to temperature increases.
She claimed that the Sustainable Data Centre Development Guidelines issued by the Investment, Trade and Industry Ministry and the Malaysian Investment Development Authority (Mida) only emphasise energy and water efficiency.
However, specific risks, expectations, forecasts, and impacts of temperature increases are not addressed in the guidelines, she said.
Additionally, the Housing and Local Government Ministry, through the Town and Country Planning Department (PLANMalaysia), prepared Data Centre Planning Guidelines to standardise planning application and approval processes.
The document stipulates a requirement to establish a 50-metre buffer zone from the data centre building line to the boundary of residential lots.
"SAM questions whether a distance of 50m — roughly the length of a school running track or an Olympic swimming pool — is truly sufficient to ensure residents do not experience temperature increases, directly or indirectly, from large-scale AI data centre operations," she said.
Based on SAM's review, data centres are not listed as Prescribed Activities requiring an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) under the Environmental Quality (Prescribed Activities) (Environmental Impact Assessment) Order 2015 currently in force.
SAM views this as a major gap in Malaysia's data centre governance, advocating that national laws keep pace with technological advancements and new infrastructure developments.
"SAM proposes that the EIA framework be amended and expanded to include emerging infrastructure and technology categories as Prescribed Activities.
"This step is essential to ensure large-scale data centre development projects undergo environmental impact assessments that mandate public displays and feedback, in line with principles of transparency and accountability in environmental management," she said.
When asked if SAM had received complaints from residents regarding AI data centre developments, she said no formal complaints had been received so far.
However, she stressed that the absence of complaints does not mean there are no risks or impacts.
"The primary action now is to ensure stricter and more effective governance and regulatory measures are implemented early, before the impacts of large-scale AI development grow into an environmental crisis too complex to handle.
"Further research is still needed. This points to the necessity for deeper socio-technical research, including field studies in areas such as Johor, which is currently becoming an AI data centre hub," she said.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Trump: AI data centre opponents want US to be 'backwards and poor'
Article:
WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump on Monday attacked opponents of artificial intelligence data centres, saying they would end up "backwards and poor" and were helping rival China.
A backlash against the energy-guzzling centres has become a surprise issue in November's US midterm elections, with Trump at odds with many Republicans.
Polls show a majority of Americans are now against building the centres, amid complaints about rising electricity bills and noise from the facilities.
"The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data centres is if they want to end up being backwards and poor," Trump said on his Truth Social platform.
"If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign," Trump said.
"If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame."
Republicans are already at risk of losing control of Congress in the midterms as the Iran war drives up the cost of living, and the data centres are proving a fresh headache.
Opposition to the facilities is growing, according to opinion polls.
A Fox News survey in July showed that 70 per cent of respondents opposed the building of an AI data centre in their area – including 60 per cent of Republicans and 76 per cent of Democrats.
And US candidates in at least 21 races across 18 states have aired television advertisements mentioning data centres this cycle, according to marketing data cited by US media, almost evenly divided between both parties.
But Trump has maintained his support, even as his administration earlier this year signed up top tech firms to a voluntary "Ratepayer Protection Pledge" to protect consumers from higher power prices.
- 'CHINA COULD NOT BE HAPPIER' -
US media reports have suggested that China may also be trying to stoke opposition to data centres, with a congressional committee demanding an investigation.
Trump, who is due to host Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House in September, did not repeat the allegation but said Beijing would be pleased with the situation.
"China could not be happier with this anti Data Centre movement. Actually, they can't believe it is happening!" Trump said.
China is on course to nearly double its data centre capacity within the next five years, as an AI race with the United States intensifies.
Trump's Vice President JD Vance – who is widely considered a possible 2028 presidential hopeful – took a more measured tone as he headed on a campaign visit to Michigan on Monday.
"Probably 99 per cent of the backlash to data centres has come in areas where building a data centre means higher utility and higher electricity," Vance told reporters.
"If you build a data centre, you should be putting power back into the grid, not taking it out. And if that is happening, I don't think the data centres are that controversial."
The White House noted in a statement about Vance's visit that OpenAI, Oracle, and Related Digital were investing more than US$7 billion in a "hyperscale data centre campus" in Michigan.
Vance is a former tech investor with close ties to Silicon Valley figures who would be expected to bankroll any presidential run after the midterms.
But at the same time, the author of the bestselling "Hillbilly Elegy" has built his political brand on his blue-collar roots and on recognising the economic concerns of US voters.--AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Fast-fashion giant Shein set to open flat in Hong Kong market debut
Article:
HONG KONG: Shares in fast-fashion giant Shein were set to open flat in their Hong Kong market debut on Tuesday, following numerous setbacks that have long delayed its listing and undermined the foundations of its business.
Known globally for selling US$5 tops and US$10 dresses, Shein has been hit by tariff and duty changes in the US and Europe.
In 2022, it was one of the world's most valuable start-ups, worth an estimated US$100 billion, but last week's initial public offering valued the company at about US$26.5 billion.
Shein also failed to list in New York and London, hampered by intense scrutiny of its business practices in the West and blocked by Chinese authorities.

Title: GOF seizes 6,000 smuggled Thai saplings worth RM300,000 in Rantau Panjang
Article:
RANTAU PANJANG: The General Operations Force (GOF) seized 6,000 plant saplings believed to have been smuggled from Thailand in Kampung Padang Licin here yesterday.
GOF Battalion 8 personnel also arrested a 61-year-old local lorry driver during the inspection at 12.45pm.
GOF Southeast Brigade commander Senior Assistant Commissioner Ahmad Radzi Hussain said the seizure occurred after officers intercepted a lorry driven by the senior citizen under suspicious circumstances.
"An inspection of the lorry led to the discovery of 6,000 Malay gooseberry, frangipani, and cactus plants.
"We seized all the plants along with the lorry, with the total seizure value estimated at RM300,000," he said in a statement.
Initial investigations revealed that the suspect had been involved in smuggling activities for the past five years and worked for a Thai man known as Salleh.
"The suspect received RM300 for each delivery of saplings to a nursery in Kedah," he said.
The seized items were handed over to the Kota Baru Agriculture Department for further action.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Brazil, US resume negotiations on Trump tariffs
Article:
BRASÍLIA: Brazil has resumed talks with the United States over the steep trade tariffs imposed by Washington, the government in Brasilia said Monday.
Washington in July imposed two new sets of tariffs on the Latin American giant, claiming unfair trade practices and use of forced labour, charging 25 per cent on some goods and 12.5 per cent on others.
Leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who is seeking a fourth term in October elections, has accused the United States of using the tariffs to interfere in the election campaign.
Lula is running against Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of Brazil's jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, a close ally of US President Donald Trump, and contends that the levies are attempt to sway voters to elect his Washington-allied opponent.
During a recent call with Trump, Lula said the grounds for the tariffs were "based on a lie."
In a follow-up call Monday with US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira and Trade Minister Marcio Elias Rosa reiterated Brazil's objections to the "discriminatory " tariffs, while adding that Brasilia was ready to continue talks.
This is the second time in as many years that the United States has imposed steep tariffs on Brazil.
Last year, it imposed 50 levies in retaliation for a trial that sent Bolsonaro to prison on charges of coup-plotting.
Those tariffs were largely reversed later on.--AFP

Title: Asia's refined fuel imports hit post-war low, can the Middle East help?
Article:
LAUNCESTON: The crisis created by the Iran conflict in the supply of refined fuels in Asia continued in August, with the top-consuming region's imports dropping to the lowest point since the war started.
Asia's imports of light and middle distillates are estimated at 5.10 million barrels per day (bpd) in August, falling from 5.61 million bpd in July, according to data compiled by Kpler, a commodities analyst.
Imports are down about 2.0 million bpd from the average of 7.06 million bpd in the three months leading up to February 28, when the US and Israel launched aerial strikes against Iran.
Since the start of the conflict much of the market focus has been on the supply of crude, given the massive drop in shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway through which nearly 20 per cent of global oil supplies moved prior to the hostilities.
Tanker movements through the strait remained constrained, though there is debate about how much oil is getting through, with claims by the US Energy Secretary of up to 9 million bpd being disputed by several vessel-tracking services, which see less than half that amount.
But the debate over crude volumes leaving the Middle East is not the argument the oil market should be pursuing, at least not in the immediate term.
Asia, the destination for about 90 per cent of Middle East crude, has adjusted to lower oil supplies, mainly with top buyer China slashing its imports by nearly 4 million bpd and also by drawing down on inventories.
But the real pressure is in the market for refined products, particularly for middle distillates like diesel and jet fuel.
The product market is having to deal with the loss of cargoes from the Middle East and also from Russia, which has curtailed fuel shipments after Ukraine successfully struck several of its refineries.
The constrained supplies of refined fuels are showing up in prices, with Singapore gasoil ending at US$155.15 a barrel on Monday, up 70 per cent from where it was - US$91.42 - on February 27, the day before the Iran war started.
The profit margin for a typical Singapore refinery to produce a barrel of gasoil ended at US$67.93 on Monday, three times more than the US$21.90 that prevailed on February 27.
Gasoline shows a similar dynamic, with the profit
for making a barrel of the light motor fuel ending last week at US$27.47, more than three times the US$8.00 from the day before the conflict started.
The wide margins for producing light and middle distillates do raise some questions about the market's dynamics.
The main question is why are Gulf producers running risks in shipping crude through both the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb waterway when they could make vastly more money moving refined products?
Exports of light and middle distillates from the Middle East are estimated by Kpler at 2.14 million bpd in August, down from 2.58 million bpd in July.
They are also 55 per cent below the 4.49 million bpd average for the three months to the end of February.
In effect, Asia's imports of light and middle distillates are down by about 2 million bpd, reflecting almost exactly the loss of supply from the Middle East.
The initial phases of the Iran war did see Tehran attack refining sites across the Gulf, but much of the damage has been repaired, although some capacity remains offline.
But it is likely that Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have the refining capacity available to produce fuels that are needed in Asia.
The problem may lie in the lack of available vessels to transport products and the difficulty in doing ship-to-ship transfers, assuming you can get the fuel out of the Strait of Hormuz without being attacked by Iranian missiles or drones.
But the one thing that the Iran conflict has reinforced is that the oil market is remarkably adept at adapting to challenging circumstances.
If Middle East producers can pivot to exporting more fuels, that would go some way to alleviating the stress in refined products markets and the risk of serious economic damage from high prices and constrained supply.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Trump says Strait of Hormuz in 'extremely good shape'
Article:
HAMILTON: US President Donald Trump said Monday that the Strait of Hormuz is in "extremely good shape," claiming US naval assistance has helped an average of 30 ships pass through each night, Anadolu Ajansi reported,
"We have the Strait of Hormuz in extremely good shape. You know, we're taking over," Trump told reporters at the Oval Office.
"Many, many ships got through last night. As you know, with the Navy's assistance, and we've been averaging 30 ships a night.
That's a lot, and a lot of oil coming out. That's why you haven't seen the price of oil go like they thought it might have to go," he said.

Title: FKLI poised to test 1,700 support, says RHB Research
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI futures contract (FKLI) is poised to test the 1,700-point support level amid continued selling pressure, according to RHB Research.
In a note, the firm said the FKLI fell 23 points to close at 1,700 points last Friday, after opening at 1,722.50 points and hitting an intraday high of 1,732 points before falling to a low of 1,693.50 points.
It said the technical setup had weakened after the FKLI breached its 50-day simple moving average (SMA) line.
"If selling pressure follows through, the FKLI may pull back towards 1,680 points. However, we expect the bulls not to cede the 1,680-point support," RHB Research said.
It added that the FKLI would resume its upward trend if it reclaimed the 50-day SMA, maintaining a positive trading bias during the current consolidation phase.
Meanwhile, crude palm oil futures (FCPO) resumed their upward movement on Friday, gaining RM78 to close at RM4,894.
RHB Research said the positive price action, coupled with a rising relative strength index (RSI), indicated that the uptrend was gaining strength.
"If the rebound persists, the commodity may climb further towards the RM5,000 resistance.
"An upward breakout should lead to a higher resistance level of RM5,100 and boost market sentiment," it said.
The firm said the correction in FCPO was deemed to have ended following the formation of a bullish candlestick after the contract rejected levels near its 50-day SMA.
It maintained a positive trading bias on the commodity.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Malaysia's manufacturing sector posts slight improvement in August: PMI data
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The seasonally adjusted S&P Global Malaysia Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) posted above the neutral mark of 50.0 that separates growth from contraction for a third straight month in August.
For August, Malaysia's PMI stood at 50.2, down from 50.7 in both July and June, signalling only a slight improvement in the health of the Malaysian manufacturing sector and one which was the weakest in the aforementioned sequence.
"The historical relationship between the PMI and official data indicates that gross domestic product and manufacturing output growth should improve in the third quarter of 2026," S&P Global said in a statement today.
It said Malaysian manufacturers recorded a third consecutive monthly rise in new orders; however, the expansion was only marginal and the weakest in the current growth sequence, due to a slowdown in new orders broadly consistent with those weighing on output.
Nonetheless, S&P Global said sustained growth in new orders encouraged some firms to expand their payrolls; as a result, August marked the first rise in employment in four months, with manufacturers taking on both full- and part-time staff.
"Amid subdued demand conditions, manufacturers remained divided in their operating trends.
"Employment rose for the first time in four months, while purchasing activity declined for the first time in five months as firms drew on inventories to meet demand requirements," said S&P Global Market Intelligence economist Maryam Baluch.
Looking ahead, she noted that confidence remained muted, suggesting that current challenging conditions are likely to persist over the coming year.
"However, softer price pressures could give firms some scope to support demand growth and, in turn, lift production," said Maryam.
Meanwhile, Malaysian manufacturers continued to face longer lead times for inputs, with poor weather conditions, low stock availability and port congestion cited as the main factors behind delays, but the incidence of delays was only slight and the least pronounced in seven months, S&P Global said.
Turning to prices, it said both input costs and output charges rose modestly in August, with inflation rates easing further.
"In fact, the rates of increase were the weakest in six months and historically subdued.
"Where prices did rise, firms attributed this to higher fuel and raw material costs, which were then often passed through to customers," S&P Global said.
It added that Malaysian manufacturers were generally confident output would rise over the coming year; however, positive sentiment remained historically weak and broadly unchanged from July.
Optimism was generally centred on hopes that demand will continue to improve, S&P Global said.

Title: Ringgit opens lower amid elevated US treasury yields
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The ringgit opened lower against the US dollar on Tuesday amid elevated US Treasury yields and uncertainty over the US Federal Reserve's (Fed) interest rate outlook, said an analyst.
At 8am, the local currency eased to 4.0300/0350 against the greenback from last Friday's close of 4.0230/0270.
Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said the 30-year US Treasury bond yield has been rising persistently to 5.25 per cent, amid expectations that the Fed could maintain a cautious stance on interest rates at the upcoming Federal Open Market Committee meeting on September 15-16.
"This happened following Fed chairman Kevin Warsh's speech on Friday at the Jackson Hole Symposium, where he explicitly indicated that inflation remains high while the labour market remains healthy.
"This seems to be a cue for raising interest rates, which appears to be in contradiction with the US Treasury Department's aim of lowering long-term bond yields through its buyback plans," he told Bernama.
This week, Mohd Afzanizam said the focus will be on the release of Nonfarm Payroll (NFP) data points, with consensus estimates showing a recovery of 58,000 in August after witnessing job losses of 23,000 in the prior month.
On another note, he said the ringgit is expected to remain cautious against the US dollar amid the resumption of military attacks between the US and Iran, which had pushed Brent crude prices higher to US$90.49 per barrel.
"Hence, the US dollar-ringgit pair is likely to range between 4.02 and 4.04 today," he added.
At the opening, the ringgit traded mostly higher against a basket of major currencies.
The ringgit strengthened against the British pound to 5.4594/4662 from last Friday's close of 5.4632/4687 and appreciated against the euro to 4.6817/6875 from 4.6828/6874, but depreciated against the Japanese yen to 2.5222/5255 from 2.5193/5219.
The local note traded mostly lower against regional currencies.
It fell against the Singapore dollar to 3.1702/1747 from 3.1652/1686 and was little changed against the Indonesian rupiah to 227.3/227.8 from 227.3/227.7 on Friday.
However, it rose against the Thai baht to 12.1525/1738 from 12.2087/2253 but remained flat against the Philippine peso at 6.46/6.47.

Title: MBPP cracks down on foreigners trading, slaughtering chickens
Article:
GEORGE TOWN: The Penang Island City Council (MBPP) will take stern action against premises allegedly used by foreigners to trade and slaughter chickens, following complaints.
MBPP mayor Datuk A. Rajendran said the council had conducted enforcement operations against the premises several times, including sealing them for two weeks.
"We have taken enforcement action a few times on these shops, even to the extent of sealing them for two weeks. The operation stops for some time but starts again due to the demand.
"It is more prominent during the weekends when the foreign workers are on leave, and they come in large numbers.
"We have been watching them for a few weeks now and gathered evidence. This time the action will be stiff," he said when contacted.
Rajendran was responding to two TikTok posts by NGO Team Surplus Pulau Pinang and KL/Selangor, which alleged that foreigners were openly flouting regulations and questioned MBPP's enforcement efforts.
One post claimed Team Surplus members had conducted an operation targeting foreigners in the Jalan Macalister area in George Town ahead of National Day.
One post claimed Team Surplus members had conducted an operation targeting foreigners along Jalan Macalister here ahead of National Day.
Another post, captioned "Komtar bukan zon kebal undang-undang", alleged that foreigners were openly violating the law in front of Komtar and questioned the consistency of enforcement action.
The posts called for greater transparency, consistency, and immediate action from the local authority to ensure regulations were enforced without discrimination and to restore public confidence in enforcement institutions.
The allegations also included claims that foreigners were allowed to trade without signboards and slaughter chickens at the premises.
Rajendran said MBPP had been monitoring the activities for several weeks and had gathered evidence before taking further action.

Title: Sarawak haze worsens, Serian records hazardous API of 415
Article:
KUCHING: Haze conditions in Sarawak have worsened, with five areas recording hazardous Air Pollutant Index (API) levels, led by Serian at 415 as of 6am today.
Data from the Department of Environment's Air Pollutant Index Management System (APIMS) showed Kuching recorded an API of 405, followed by Samarahan (369), Sri Aman (355), and Sarikei (328).
Four other areas recorded very unhealthy levels: Sibu (298), Mukah (228), Bintulu (221), and Samalaju (218).
Meanwhile, four areas recorded unhealthy levels, led by ILP Miri at 184, followed by Miri (178), Kapit (176), and Limbang (166).
The worsening haze is expected to heighten health risks, particularly for vulnerable groups such as children, the elderly, pregnant women, and individuals with respiratory issues or lung conditions.
Yesterday, Sarawak Deputy Premier Datuk Amar Dr Sim Kui Hian revealed that the average number of Upper Respiratory Tract Infection (URTI) cases in Sarawak rose from about 1,717 cases a week early this year to 1,752 cases a week in recent weeks following deteriorating air quality since early August.
He said conjunctivitis cases also increased to an average of 21 cases a week compared to 17 previously.

Title: Unidentified body found in drain, police suspect murder
Article:
SUNGAI BULOH: The body of an unidentified man, believed to be a murder victim, was found in a drain along Jalan Industri 7 in Kampung Baru Sungai Buloh near here on Aug 29.
District police chief Superintendent Mohd Hafiz Muhammad Nor said police were alerted to the discovery by members of the public, and the Fire and Rescue Department was enlisted to assist in retrieving the body.
He said the body was subsequently sent to the Sungai Buloh Hospital for a post-mortem examination.
"Preliminary checks revealed no identification documents on the deceased, and his identity has yet to be established.
"The deceased is a fair-skinned man, bald, standing about 170cm tall and weighing 50kg," he said in a statement today.
He added that the post-mortem results revealed elements of crime on the victim's body, leading police to classify the case under Section 302 of the Penal Code for murder.
"Further investigations are underway to identify the victim and track down the suspects involved," he said.
He urged members of the public with information on the incident, or those with missing family members matching the victim's description, to contact the investigating officer, Assistant Superintendent Mohd Reezal Mohammad @ Mohd Zain, at 013-3479809.
Information can also be relayed to the Sungai Buloh district police headquarters at 03-61561222 or any nearby police station.

Title: Four killed in crash involving 11 vehicles near Temerloh
Article:
TEMERLOH: Four people, including three family members, were killed and three others injured in an 11-vehicle crash at Km110.4 of the East Coast Expressway 1 (LPT 1) near the Temerloh toll plaza exit last night.
The 10pm incident involved a tanker truck, an express bus, four cars, three sports utility vehicles (SUVs), a multi-purpose vehicle (MPV), and a pickup truck.
Pahang Fire and Rescue Department operations division assistant director Mohd Salahuddin Isa said the driver and two passengers of an SUV died at the scene.
He said the crash also claimed the life of a man travelling in another SUV.
"All the victims killed in the accident were trapped in their vehicles, and firefighters took over an hour to extricate them," he said.
"Two other victims, involving the tanker driver and a man in an SUV, were seriously injured. All 30 passengers on the express bus escaped unhurt," he said when contacted.
"The accident occurred while all vehicles were travelling from Kuala Lumpur towards Kuantan. Police are still investigating the cause of the crash," he added.
Salahuddin said all four bodies were sent to the Sultan Ahmad Shah Hospital here for post-mortem examinations, adding that the identities of the deceased have yet to be confirmed.
He added that the two injured victims were also sent to the same hospital for treatment.

Title: Rare black bass caught in Penang river after 15 years
Article:
GEORGE TOWN: A rare black bass, locally known as ikan kanai or tembaring, was caught by a local fisherman at Sungai Kuala, after the species reportedly went unrecorded in the area for about 15 years.
The Penang Fisheries Department said the catch on Aug 30 was significant as local fishermen had not reported seeing the species in the area for about 15 years.
In a Facebook post, the department identified the fish as Lutjanus goldiei, a predatory estuarine species known for its strength and endurance, making it a prized sport fish.
The department said the species was more commonly found in estuarine areas in Sabah and Papua New Guinea, making its presence in Penang noteworthy in terms of its geographical distribution.
It said L. goldiei typically inhabits tidal estuaries and coastal riverine areas, particularly those with mangrove and nipa vegetation that provide shelter and feeding grounds.
"The discovery at Sungai Kuala suggests that the area can provide suitable ecological conditions for the species," it said.
The department also said that L. goldiei is a native species and should not be confused with the introduced largemouth bass (Micropterus salmoides) reported in other areas.
"As the species is rarely encountered and considered sensitive to environmental changes, we encourage anglers and fishermen to practise catch-and-release to support conservation efforts and maintain sustainable populations in Malaysian waters," it added.

Title: Before the Sky Turns Grey
Article:
There are some visitors who arrive without warning. El Niño is not one of them. We watch it developing across the Pacific - meteorologists track the oceans, weather agencies issue forecasts, plantation managers watch rainfall and farmers the sky.
Yet when the land dries, fires break out and haze drifts across Southeast Asia, we still behave as though nature has surprised us.
And so, here we are again in 2026. Indonesia is battling widespread forest and land fires, haze has crossed borders and Sarawak has again felt the consequences.
Firefighting, cloud seeding and ground operations have intensified. Arrests have been made, companies investigated and sanctions imposed. Good. Where laws are broken, act. Where deliberate burning occurs, prosecute. Where negligence allows fire to spread, establish responsibility.
But there is a larger question: If we knew the dry weather was coming, what did we do before the fire started?
Southeast Asia is hardly new to haze. We have decades of experience, satellite technology, weather forecasting, peatland research, regulations and regional cooperation.
Yet every dry season, the storyline remains familiar: red dots appear, smoke rises, air-quality readings worsen, helicopters arrive and everyone starts looking for the match.
El Niño makes conditions hotter and drier, but El Niño does not carry a match. Weather creates risk. Human decisions determine much of what follows. That is why the bigger shift must be from proving yesterday's blame to preventing tomorrow's fire.
A hotspot is also not a guilty verdict. Satellite detection tells us where unusual heat is occurring; it does not automatically tell us who started the fire, whether it began inside a concession or spread in from outside, or whether the landholder was fighting rather than causing it.
Satellites are very clever. They have yet to acquire a law degree. So investigate first. Follow the evidence. If it leads to a plantation company, follow it there. If it leads to a contractor, smallholder, illegal land clearer, arsonist or land dispute, follow it there too.
Sometimes the precise origin may never be established with certainty. Accountability matters, but so does fairness. Punish the guilty, certainly - but do not condemn an entire sector by association.
The more important test, however, is what happens before a fire becomes a regional emergency.
When fires become large, the response can look impressive: helicopters, water bombing, cloud seeding and thousands of personnel. All may be necessary.
But perhaps the better measure is not how much we mobilise after disaster strikes, but how many dangerous fires never became large enough to need such mobilisation. The first 24 hours matter.
When a hotspot appears, who receives the alert? How quickly is it verified? Who gets there first? Is there water? Are the pumps working? How much time passes before suppression begins?
A satellite hundreds of kilometers overhead can detect the heat. It would be embarrassing if the information then spent hours finding the correct department or landowner.
Satellite speed above; meeting speed below. Perhaps we need to move beyond hotspot maps to response maps - tracking not only where fires occur, but how quickly they are verified and contained.
Fire also does not recognise boundaries. It cannot read a land title, distinguish plantation land from customary land or stop at a district border. The real unit of fire prevention must therefore be the landscape, not merely individual properties.
Plantations can contribute roads, pumps, machinery and trained people; communities bring local knowledge. Technology has eyes in the sky, local people have eyes on the ground. We need both.
The same realism applies to smallholders. Fire is cheap; mechanical clearing is not. If society wants fire-free land preparation, the alternative must be affordable. A "No Open Burning" sign helps, but an affordable alternative may persuade more than prohibition alone.
So yes, count hotspots, hectares burned, arrests and prosecutions. But also count response time, fires contained within the first day and, most importantly, how many potentially serious fires remained small.
That measures preparedness rather than disaster. We are not short of knowledge. We know the dry season comes, we know the vulnerable landscapes, and we have the satellites, forecasts, machinery and laws.
The question is whether we act before the sky turns grey.
Because by the time smoke reaches our cities, prevention has already lost. El Niño doesn't carry a match. But neither does it accept excuses.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: US trade curbs put Malaysia's solar, semiconductor ambitions to the test
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The latest United States (US) trade measures on polysilicon pose risks for Malaysia's solar industry but could create opportunities for its semiconductor sector.
The measures, announced by US President Donald Trump last week, include a 15 per cent tariff and minimum import prices for polysilicon and its derivatives, including ingots, wafers, solar cells and modules.
The measures will take effect on Dec 4.
The policy is aimed at strengthening US domestic manufacturing and reducing reliance on China in supply chains considered critical to solar panels, semiconductors, artificial intelligence (AI) and energy security.
For Malaysia, the implications are unlikely to be uniform.
The bigger question is whether the country can turn these global shifts into higher-value opportunities rather than simply becoming another destination for relocated manufacturing.
A Trade Measure With A Much Bigger Price Tag
The significance of the US move becomes clearer when the new minimum price is compared with prevailing global market prices.
According to Bernreuter Research, the proposed US minimum import price for polysilicon is US$21 per kilogramme (kg), while the current global polysilicon spot price is around US$4.78 per kg.
That means the US price floor is more than four times the prevailing spot price, potentially altering the economics of supplying the US market.
The measures come as China continues to dominate the upstream solar supply chain, particularly in polysilicon and wafer production.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) data shows China accounts for more than 80 per cent of global polysilicon manufacturing capacity, with its share of upstream solar components approaching 90 per cent.
Such concentration has made the solar supply chain increasingly vulnerable to trade restrictions, geopolitical tensions and disruptions.
For Washington, the latest measures are therefore not simply about raising import costs.
They form part of a broader attempt to encourage domestic production of strategic materials and reduce dependence on Chinese-dominated supply chains.
For countries such as Malaysia, however, the question is whether being outside China is enough to attract the next wave of investment.
The answer, according to industry representatives, is becoming increasingly complicated.
Malaysia Is Not Just A Solar Deployment Market
One of the more important findings from industry feedback is that Malaysia's solar industry cannot simply be categorised as a deployment market.
According to data from the Malaysian Investment Development Authority (MIDA), Malaysia has an almost complete solar ecosystem comprising about 250 companies.
Its covers upstream activities such as polysilicon, wafer, cell and module production, as well as downstream activities including inverters, balance-of-system components and system integration.
But the Malaysia Photovoltaic and Sustainable Energy Industry Association (MPSEA) told Business Times that the figure should not be interpreted as 250 manufacturers.
"The figure covers the wider solar ecosystem, including a relatively small number of large multinational manufacturers, as well as local developers, engineering, procurement, construction, and commissioning contractors (EPCC), consultants, distributors, installers, system integrators, operations and maintenance (O&M) providers and other service providers," it said.
In other words, MPSEA said Malaysia has two complementary solar industries.
The first is an export-oriented manufacturing base dominated mainly by multinational companies.
The second is a growing domestic deployment and services ecosystem driven by Large Scale Solar (LSS), rooftop solar, the Corporate Renewable Energy Supply Scheme (CRESS), corporate renewable-energy demand and increasingly, energy storage.
This distinction could become increasingly important as US trade policy changes the economics of exporting solar products.
"Malaysia remains a manufacturing hub, but future industry growth will increasingly depend on domestic and regional deployment, higher local participation, technology development and moving beyond basic manufacturing or assembly into higher-value activities," it said.
The Solar Manufacturing Dilemma
MPSEA's assessment is notably less optimistic about the immediate impact of the new US measures.
The association said the measures are global in application and are not specifically directed at Malaysia.
"Nevertheless, Malaysia is directly relevant because the country hosts an established solar manufacturing ecosystem, including solar-grade polysilicon production in Samalaju, Sarawak, as well as integrated ingot, wafer, cell and module manufacturing in Kuching and other industrial locations.
"The immediate concern is that Malaysia is not presently listed among the countries receiving differentiated tariff treatment.
"As a result, Malaysian exports of covered solar products to the US may be subject to both the applicable minimum import price requirements and the additional tariff," it said.
Even companies using non-Chinese polysilicon may not automatically be exempt, making origin verification and supply-chain documentation increasingly important.
This is where the issue moves beyond tariffs.
For solar manufacturers, the next competitive battle may increasingly be about traceability.
MPSEA said buyers are likely to place greater emphasis on regulatory compliance, supply-chain transparency, product origin and long-term supply security rather than selecting suppliers purely on price.
Malaysia has some advantages.
The country has an established non-China manufacturing base, while Sarawak's hydropower resources could support lower-carbon production.
"However, this advantage will only be meaningful if Malaysian products can demonstrate transparent origin, low-carbon manufacturing and compliance throughout the supply chain," said MPSEA.
The Price Floor Could Reshape Sourcing Decisions
The proposed US price floor could also influence investment decisions well beyond Malaysia.
MPSEA said the gap between the proposed US minimum price and prevailing global prices is large enough to materially influence sourcing decisions for the US market.
"Buyers will increasingly prioritise regulatory compliance, supply-chain traceability, product origin and long-term supply security, rather than selecting suppliers solely based on the lowest price.
"It may also accelerate investment in US-based polysilicon, ingot, wafer and cell manufacturing, particularly because the measures provide incentives for companies committing to onshore production," it said.
For Malaysia, that creates a mixed picture.
The country's non-China manufacturing base and hydropower-supported polysilicon production could provide strategic value.
But Malaysian manufacturers are not automatically exempt from the measures.
This means Malaysia could find itself caught between two competing forces: an opportunity to provide a non-China source of supply, but also the risk of losing competitiveness in the US market if its products face the same tariff and price requirements as other foreign suppliers.
MPSEA said the government should therefore engage the US authorities to seek recognition of Malaysia as a reliable, transparent and lower-carbon supply-chain partner.
Outside the US, it noted that displaced supply may be redirected to Asia and other markets, potentially increasing competition and placing further downward pressure on global prices.
"Therefore, Malaysia must diversify its export markets while strengthening domestic demand and moving towards higher-value, traceable and technologically advanced solar products," it said.
Demand May Be Stronger Than The Trade Shock
Despite the risks facing solar manufacturers, the outlook for solar deployment in Malaysia is considerably less alarming.
Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said there could be a knee-jerk reaction initially as US businesses adjust to higher import tariffs.
He said the move was intended partly to encourage US companies to meet domestic demand, but expanding domestic production would take time.
Existing US players would need to scale up and incur capital expenditure to improve their production capacity, he said.
More importantly, however, the underlying demand for energy continues to grow rapidly with the proliferation of AI and data centres globally.
Afzanizam pointed to data centre electricity demand in Malaysia, with load utilisation rising to 1,054 megawatts (MW) in the first quarter (Q1) of 2026 from 190MW in the Q2 2024, a 5.5-fold increase.
The surge matters for renewable energy because the expansion of data centres is increasing pressure on electricity supply and the need for a diversified energy mix.
"Certainly, the energy mix coming from RE is extremely critical and that includes solar," he said.
Against that backdrop, he does not expect the latest US measures to have a major impact on the broader solar industry.
He said demand for renewable energy, particularly solar, is continuing to rise domestically.
"The impact is there, but I don't think it will crash the market," he added.
That distinction is important.
The US measures could hurt the economics of exporting certain solar products to America without necessarily undermining the economics of installing solar systems in Malaysia.
For developers and installers focused on the domestic market, the bigger drivers remain electricity demand, corporate renewable-energy commitments, government programmes and the growing need for additional power capacity.
Semiconductors Offer A Different Opportunity
If the solar industry faces a more defensive challenge, Malaysia's semiconductor industry appears to be entering the latest period of supply-chain disruption from a position of relative strength.
Malaysia Semiconductor Industry Association (MSIA) president Datuk Seri Wong Siew Hai said Malaysia is well positioned to capture a larger share of the global semiconductor value chain, backed by more than five decades of experience in semiconductor manufacturing and outsourced semiconductor assembly and testing (OSAT).
"The country also has established global supply-chain linkages and a deep supporting ecosystem," he told the Business Times.
According to the data from MIDA, Malaysia accounts for about seven per cent of global semiconductor trade and 13 per cent of global chip assembly, testing and packaging activities, while ranking as the world's sixth-largest semiconductor exporter.
More importantly, Malaysia is already seeing a significant investment response.
The semiconductor sector attracted about RM91.9 billion in approved investments between January 2024 and March 2026.
This comprises RM82.9 billion in foreign direct investment and RM8.9 billion in domestic investment, according to Investment, Trade and Industry Ministry figures reported in Parliament.
That investment momentum suggests global companies are already treating Malaysia as more than simply a low-cost manufacturing base.
"The areas that stand to benefit most are advanced packaging, IC design and R&D, semiconductor equipment and supporting technologies, specialised areas such as power semiconductors, and digitally enabled manufacturing.
"The growth in AI and high-performance computing is creating demand across the entire value chain, from memory and advanced packaging to equipment and supporting technologies," said Wong.
The Next Battle Is Higher Up The Value Chain
Wong said global disruptions since the first US-China trade tensions have changed how companies manage their supply chains, with greater emphasis on risk mitigation, resilience and diversification.
That creates opportunities for Malaysian companies, particularly SMEs, to deepen their participation in global supply chains.
"The longer-term ambition is to develop and build our own capabilities and IP, allowing Malaysian companies to capture greater value and move further up the semiconductor value chain," he said.
Opportunities are also emerging in wide-bandgap semiconductors, memory and AI-related technologies.
This is where Malaysia's semiconductor strategy could diverge sharply from its solar manufacturing story.
In solar, Malaysia already has substantial manufacturing capacity but faces the risk that global trade rules could make some export markets less attractive.
In semiconductors, meanwhile, global supply-chain diversification could create demand for exactly the capabilities Malaysia is trying to develop.
A More Demanding Global Landscape
Malaysia Equities chief information officer Lee Chun Hong said Malaysia's solar manufacturing sector could face increasing challenges as US policy intensifies efforts to reduce reliance on Chinese-dominated supply chains.
Lee said Malaysian manufacturers could face higher compliance costs if locally manufactured solar products contain imported polysilicon or Chinese-origin intermediate components destined for the US market.
"In addition, there is a growing risk of heightened scrutiny around rules-of-origin requirements, particularly as policymakers seek to prevent the circumvention of measures aimed at limiting China's influence across the solar value chain," he said.
But Lee sees a more constructive medium-term outlook for semiconductors.
As US and multinational companies continue to diversify production networks away from China, Lee said Malaysia is well positioned to capture a greater share of investment flows aimed at enhancing supply chain resilience.
He expects this trend to support further expansion of Malaysia's semiconductor ecosystem, particularly in established technology clusters such as Penang and Kulim.
The contrast is increasingly difficult to ignore.
The same global supply-chain diversification that creates uncertainty for one Malaysian industry could create an opportunity for another.
The Malaysia Question
The bigger question, however, is whether Malaysia can capture the value of this shift rather than simply host another generation of factories.
Its solar ecosystem stretches from upstream polysilicon to downstream deployment, while its semiconductor industry has spent more than five decades building relationships with global manufacturers.
For solar, MPSEA said Malaysia needs to strengthen domestic demand, upstream and downstream integration, research and development, local participation and export-market diversification.
For semiconductors, MSIA said Malaysia's longer-term ambition should be to develop its own capabilities and intellectual property to capture greater value and move further up the semiconductor value chain.
The message running through all these sectors is therefore similar, even if their immediate prospects differ.
The latest developments suggest that supply-chain diversification alone may not automatically translate into gains for Malaysia.
The country has to prove that it can offer something more valuable than lower costs, whether that is resilient semiconductor capacity, advanced engineering capabilities, low-carbon solar manufacturing, trusted supply chains or access to a rapidly growing regional renewable-energy market.
As AI and data centres drive higher demand for electricity and advanced computing, Malaysia's ability to capture more value from the resulting investment cycle will depend increasingly on its capabilities across both the renewable energy and semiconductor value chains.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Bank Negara seen holding OPR on Thursday as global rate pressures build
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Bank Negara Malaysia is expected to keep the overnight policy rate (OPR) unchanged at 2.75 per cent this week, with resilient domestic demand and manageable inflation giving it room to stay on the sidelines.
The expected pause comes as inflation concerns revive rate-hike risks among several major central banks, including those in New Zealand and the eurozone.
UOB Global Economics & Markets Research expects Bank Negara to maintain its "wait-and-see" stance at its Sept 3 Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting while remaining vigilant over external developments.
Economist Lee Sue Ann pointed to resilient domestic demand, ongoing government policy support, continued artificial intelligence (AI) and data centre-related investments, and sustained tourism activity.
Together with manageable inflationary pressures, these "should provide important growth buffers", she said in a note on Monday.
Bank Negara is scheduled for its fifth of six MPC meetings this year. The OPR has remained at 2.75 per cent since July 2025, when the central bank cut the benchmark rate by 25 basis points.
The case for keeping rates steady has been reinforced by Malaysia's stronger economic performance.
The economy expanded six per cent year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, supported by services and manufacturing, including the operationalisation of data centres and strong artificial intelligence-related demand for electrical and electronics exports.
Inflation, meanwhile, has remained relatively contained despite higher external cost pressures stemming from the Middle East conflict.
Headline inflation averaged 1.9 per cent in the second quarter, up from 1.6 per cent in the preceding quarter, while core inflation eased to 1.9 per cent from 2.1 per cent.
Bank Negara expects headline inflation to average between 1.5 per cent and 2.5 per cent this year.
The relatively benign domestic backdrop contrasts with a more complicated monetary policy environment elsewhere, where renewed inflation pressures are putting rate hikes back on the table.
UOB expects the Reserve Bank of New Zealand to raise its official cash rate by 25 basis points to 2.75 per cent on Sept 2, a day before Bank Negara's decision.
It said New Zealand's headline inflation of 4.1 per cent and broadening price pressures were likely to keep policymakers focused on inflation risks despite soft labour market conditions and spare capacity.
The European Central Bank is also expected to raise rates by 25 basis points on Sept 10 after pausing in July, with persistent inflation and the risk of second-round effects from higher energy prices remaining a concern.
In the United States, UOB expects the Federal Reserve to leave rates unchanged for the rest of 2026 before resuming its easing cycle next year.
However, Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh's emphasis on inflation risks at the recent Jackson Hole Symposium has raised the risk of monetary tightening this year, UOB said.
It added that the Fed's updated economic projections and "dot plot", which shows individual policymakers' projections for future interest rates, would be closely watched for clues on the future path of rates.
Elsewhere in Asia, UOB expects the Bank of Japan (BOJ) to keep rates unchanged in September, although it puts the probability of a hike at 40 per cent amid persistent inflation pressures and yen weakness.
Its base case is for the BOJ to resume tightening later in the fourth quarter with a 25-basis-point increase to 1.25 per cent.
Bank Indonesia is also expected to stay on hold at 5.75 per cent this month as it focuses on preserving rupiah stability amid volatile global markets, geopolitical uncertainty and higher energy prices.
UOB, however, views the pause as temporary, with further rate increases possible later this year if needed to support the rupiah and anchor inflation expectations.
The Reserve Bank of Australia is similarly expected to hold its cash rate at 4.35 per cent on Sept 29, although UOB said another 25-basis-point increase remained a possibility given sticky underlying inflation and resilient domestic demand.
For Malaysia, UOB's expectation of an unchanged OPR is shared by other economists.
DBS Group Research expects Bank Negara to maintain the OPR at 2.75 per cent, saying robust economic growth and contained inflation leave little urgency for the central bank to tighten monetary policy.
Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid has also said there is little reason for Bank Negara to change its policy stance at this juncture, given robust economic growth and moderate inflation.
Bank Negara's latest monetary policy decision will be announced on Thursday.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: AirBorneo weighs selling older ATRs ahead of fleet revamp in 2027
Article:
KUCHING: AirBorneo Airways Sdn Bhd (AirBorneo) is considering phasing out its older ATR aircraft as the Sarawak-owned carrier prepares to renew its turboprop fleet in the second half of 2027.
Chief executive officer, Megat Ardian Aminuddin, said the airline was examining several options for the aircraft that would leave its fleet.
"We are still discussing that, and there are a few options. Number one is to sell them outright," he told Business Times in a recent interview.
He said AirBorneo had received interest from operators and companies that could acquire the outgoing ATRs, although discussions remained at an early stage.
"It is still very early. The first replacement aircraft will arrive in the third or fourth quarter of 2027, so we still have time to finalise those arrangements," he said.
AirBorneo and turboprop manufacturer ATR announced an agreement during the Singapore Airshow 2026 for eight new ATR 600-series aircraft.
The order comprises five ATR 72-600s and three ATR 42-600s, with purchase rights for four additional aircraft. Deliveries are scheduled between 2027 and 2029.
The new aircraft will replace AirBorneo's existing ATRs on a one-for-one basis.
"The aircraft will still be used primarily for the Rural Air Services operation. It will be a one-in, one-out arrangement, a one-for-one replacement," Megat said.
AirBorneo inherited the turboprop operation from Malaysia Aviation Group subsidiary MASwings when it assumed responsibility for the airline's services on Jan 1, 2026.
The turboprops support Rural Air Services and other routes across Sarawak, Sabah and Labuan.
AirBorneo's six De Havilland Canada Twin Otters will remain in service for the time being. Megat estimated that the aircraft were about 12 to 14 years old.
The airline expects to consider replacing the Twin Otters within the next three to four years, depending on the aircraft available in the market.
The replacement could be another De Havilland aircraft or an aircraft produced by a different manufacturer, he said.
Megat added that older aircraft could be more expensive to operate, but said their continued operation depended on maintenance planning, operational resilience and efficiency.
"All of the turboprop maintenance is carried out in Malaysia," he said.

Title: AirBorneo plans wider Asian network from Kuching hub
Article:
KUCHING: AirBorneo Airways Sdn Bhd (AirBorneo) plans to develop Kuching as a network hub connecting Sarawak's rural and urban communities with Sabah, Kalimantan, Peninsular Malaysia and other regional markets.
Chief executive officer Megat Ardian Aminuddin said passengers arriving in Kuching would be able to connect to other destinations across AirBorneo's network.
"Yes, Kuching becomes the hub," he told Business Times in an exclusive interview.
AirBorneo currently operates Rural Air Services and other turboprop routes across Sarawak, Sabah and Labuan. The carrier is adding jet services as part of its expansion into domestic trunk routes and regional markets.
Megat said the network would be developed from AirBorneo's existing operations in Sarawak before expanding across Borneo and beyond.
"We have a network that is unique and very relevant to Sarawak," he said.
He said Sarawakians required air links to travel outside the state, while inbound connectivity was needed to support tourism, investment, business, medical tourism and education.
AirBorneo launched its first commercial jet service between Kuala Lumpur and Kuching on July 20, 2026. Regular twice-daily services between Kuching International Airport and Kuala Lumpur International Airport Terminal 1 began the following day.
The airline launched its first international route between Kuching and Singapore on July 22, with daily flights serving Singapore Changi Airport Terminal 4.
The two routes are operated using wet-leased Boeing 737-800 aircraft.
Megat said AirBorneo's network would initially cover destinations within Sarawak and Sabah before expanding to Indonesia, Peninsular Malaysia and other parts of Southeast Asia.
Potential destinations in Indonesia include Banjarmasin, Balikpapan and Pontianak, as well as Bali and Surabaya. AirBorneo has not announced launch dates for those routes.
The network could later extend to southern China and Northeast Asia, he said.
"We always start from where we are, the heart of Borneo, and then grow outwards," Megat said.
AirBorneo plans to carry both point-to-point and connecting passengers. It is also considering interline and codeshare arrangements with other airlines to provide connections beyond the destinations it serves directly.
When asked if Kuching International Airport could support AirBorneo's growth ambitions, Megat said the airline had shared its five-year growth plans with the airport operator, Malaysia Airports Holdings Bhd (MAHB).
"We have had very good discussions with MAHB and have shared our five-year plan with them.
"We are currently discussing how the introduction of additional aircraft will affect terminal expansion, the optimisation of the terminal and the optimisation of the aircraft bays.
"Those discussions are not only about Kuching but also the other airports that we will serve. Kuching, however, is our base. So, that is the main focus of our discussions with MAHB," he said.
Megat said AirBorneo would also use Sarawak's identity as part of its full-service offering.
"No other airline can give you the scent of Sarawak or the taste of Sarawak, with Sarawak cuisine on board. Above all, AirBorneo is the realisation of the state's vision.
"The state has allocated the working capital, operational expenditure and capital expenditure for the next few years, so the funding has already been provided for," he added.
