Title: US Army Secretary Driscoll submits resignation: White House
Article:
WASHINGTON: US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll has submitted his resignation, the White House confirmed Monday, following reports of tensions with Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Asked about a Wall Street Journal report that Driscoll had resigned, White House Principal Deputy Press Secretary Anna Kelly did not deny it.
"Driscoll has been highly effective in advancing President Trump's agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army," Kelly said.
She cited his "outstanding leadership" during US military operations, "restoring an emphasis on readiness and lethality, assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, and more."
She added: "The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War."
If accepted, Driscoll's resignation would mark the latest departure of a senior military leader under President Donald Trump administration.
A former law school classmate of Vice President JD Vance, Driscoll had reportedly benefited from their friendship within the administration, but clashed with Hegseth.
An Army veteran who served in Iraq, Driscoll ran unsuccessfully for Congress in 2020 and later advised Trump's 2024 reelection campaign.
With the Iran war entering its seventh month, the resignation could effectively leaves the Army without permanent civilian or uniformed leadership. Hegseth fired Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George in April and has yet to nominate a permanent successor.--AFP

Title: Trump vows to hit Iran hard after fresh exchange of fire
Article:
ASHEVILLE, North Carolina: US President Donald Trump threatened further strikes against Iran on Monday after the first exchange of direct attacks in a month, raising tensions in a conflict that had recently shifted into an economic standoff.
Iran launched missiles overnight at two US air bases in Jordan in response to a US attack on Iran's Larak Island, where Washington said it had struck Iranian launchers firing mines into the Strait of Hormuz.
The exchange highlighted how quickly a conflict that has increasingly been fought through sanctions, blockades and economic pressure can still spill back into military action. While neither side appeared to be seeking a return to full-scale war, both signalled they were prepared to respond to further attacks.
"We're going to hit them hard," a Fox News reporter quoted Trump as later telling the channel. "There will be a response."
Separately, Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that the renewed strikes did not signal a return to full-scale war, describing Iran as a "failed nation" whose economy and military had been severely degraded.
"That doesn't mean we won't smack them. We'll see what happens."
Asked whether he had ruled out using nuclear weapons against Iran, Trump said there was "no reason" to do so because Iran was already "totally defeated militarily."
A senior Iranian source told Reuters the overnight exchanges of fire, the first since late July, were a "limited and contained confrontation" but said Teheran would deliver a harsh response if attacked again.
Trump said US air defences had downed all Iranian missiles that could have caused any damage and that new US economic sanctions on Iran were having a big impact, Fox News reported.
Earlier, Trump had posted to social media two videos depicting explosions engulfing Iran's main oil export terminal, with the message "Kharg island being blown to smithereens!!!"
But the videos were generated by AI and no such attack took place. Iran called Trump's post "laughable." Vice President JD Vance told reporters Trump "likes to switch it up on social media a little bit" and was "sending a message."
Washington has so far mainly held off from hitting Iran's major oil and gas infrastructure, a move that Iran says would be met with devastating attacks against its Gulf neighbours.
PILING ON ECONOMIC PRESSURE
Washington has, instead, stepped up efforts to punish Teheran and its business partners with "secondary sanctions" that hit third countries buying its oil.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that Iran was "lashing out" now because the new sanctions were taking a toll on its economy.
"They're in shock at the state of their economy," Bessent told reporters at a meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bank governors in North Carolina. "I would think that they are lashing out kinetically because they are losing economically."
Bessent told Reuters on Sunday that new secondary sanctions were likely to be unveiled weekly in the effort to pressure Iran, with an initial focus on banks.
US HIT IRANIAN ISLAND IN STRAIT OF HORMUZ
US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Iran's Larak Island on Sunday, a US official said, after "Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz."
Three people were killed in the US attack, Iran's Tasnim news agency reported. The state-affiliated Nournews said two of them had been identified as members of the Revolutionary Guards Navy.
Larak is a small island in the strait near the strategic Iranian port of Bandar Abbas. The Strait of Hormuz, which normally handles a fifth of global crude oil and gas shipments, has been effectively blocked since the start of the war.
In a statement, the US Central Command said it had taken "limited, precise" action against minelaying forces of Iran's Revolutionary Guards that posed an "imminent threat" in the strait. It gave no details.
Iranian state TV quoted the Revolutionary Guards as saying a supertanker had caught fire and been brought to a halt after being struck by two naval mines in the south of the strait. The US military later denied the claim.
PRESIDENT SAYS IRAN STILL WANTS NEGOTIATED END TO CONFLICT
Trump halted his "Operation Epic Fury" bombing campaign with a ceasefire in April, and the sides agreed in June on an interim framework for talks. But that failed to hold, leading to repeated exchanges of fire including two weeks of US bombing in July.
Over the past month, Washington has hoped a blockade of Iranian ports will inflict enough economic damage to force Iran to comply with US demands. Teheran meanwhile has maintained that the Strait of Hormuz is shut and will reopen only under its supervision.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian nevertheless said on Monday that Teheran still favoured a negotiated settlement.
.".. we believe that continuing the war is in no one's interest, neither ours, nor the region's, nor humanity's," Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency quoted him as telling Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of a regional security meeting in Kyrgyzstan.
Trump has yet to achieve the objectives he set out at the start of the war: dismantling Iran's nuclear programme, curbing its ability to attack regional rivals and creating conditions for Iranians to overthrow their clerical rulers.--REUTERS
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Indonesia backs stronger Asean cooperation on transboundary haze
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Indonesia has reaffirmed its commitment to the Asean Agreement on Transboundary  Haze Pollution (AATHP), describing it as an important framework for regional cooperation in tackling transboundary haze.
Indonesian Ambassador to Malaysia Datuk Raden Mohammad Iman Hascarya Kusumo said the republic supported further strengthening regional mechanisms among Asean members.
"Indonesia remains committed to the AATHP and considers it an important framework for regional cooperation.
"Indonesia believes regional mechanisms should continue to be strengthened in terms of implementation, particularly in early warning and monitoring, real-time information and data sharing, coordination of firefighting operations, weather modification and capacity-building among Asean member states."
He said Indonesia also continued to advocate accelerating the full operationalisation of the Asean Coordinating Centre for Transboundary Haze Pollution Control to further strengthen regional coordination.
The AATHP is a legally binding regional agreement adopted by Asean member states in 2002 to prevent, monitor and mitigate transboundary haze pollution arising from land and forest fires.
The agreement requires member states to cooperate in areas including monitoring and assessment, prevention and mitigation, technical assistance, information sharing and the development of national policies to address land and forest fires.
It also provides a framework for countries to work together when haze pollution crosses national borders.
Ten Asean member states were parties to the agreement, with Indonesia becoming the final Asean country to ratify the pact in 2015, more than a decade after it was adopted.
The agreement was introduced amid recurring haze episodes in the region, particularly the severe 1997-1998 crisis, which affected several Southeast Asian countries and highlighted the need for a coordinated regional response.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Malaysia open to Asean haze pact review [WATCH]
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR:  The government is open to reviewing the Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution (AATHP) amid concerns that the bloc has yet to fully address the recurring haze problem.
The Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Ministry said a review of the more than two-decade-old agreement could be considered, but strengthening implementation of the existing framework should remain the immediate priority.
"The ministry recognises concerns over the recurring transboundary haze issue.
"While a review of the agreement may be considered, we believe the immediate priority is to strengthen the implementation of the existing AATHP," it said in a written response to the
New Straits Times
.
The AATHP is a legally binding agreement adopted by Asean member states in 2002 to prevent, monitor and mitigate transboundary haze pollution arising from land and forest fires.
Though the agreement came into force in 2003, the region still saw annual haze, with one of the worst happening in 2015.
Asean had described the event as unprecedented in severity and geographical spread, affecting Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Brunei and parts of the Philippines and Laos.
Malaysia is experiencing another bout of haze, with Air Pollutant Index (API) readings in parts of Sarawak categorised as "hazardous".
Deputy Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Minister Datuk Seri Syed Ibrahim Syed Noh said the AATHP remained an important regional framework, but its mechanisms should continue to evolve to address changing challenges.
He said the focus should not be on whether the agreement succeeded or failed, but on whether Asean members were doing enough collectively to prevent haze from recurring and respond quickly when incidents occurred.
On whether the AATHP lacked enforcement mechanisms, he said the matter should not be viewed solely from an enforcement perspective.
"While enforcement is part of the discussion, we should also look at whether the mechanisms available today are sufficient to prevent, detect and respond to these incidents effectively.
"If there are areas within the AATHP that can be strengthened, then that is a discussion Asean should have collectively.
"Any improvement should ultimately be practical, workable and capable of delivering better outcomes on the ground.
"This is not about pointing fingers. Haze does not recognise national borders and neither should our commitment to finding solutions," he told the
NST
.
The ministry said the haze problem could not be addressed through the agreement alone, as the AATHP was founded on Asean principles of consensus, mutual respect and respect for national sovereignty.
It said stronger regional cooperation and concrete action by all Asean members were needed, in line with the AATHP and the Second Asean Haze-Free Roadmap 2023-2030.
On calls for stronger enforcement mechanisms under the agreement, the ministry said enforcement remained closely tied to sovereignty, with direct enforcement dependent on countries implementing and enforcing their laws.
"Rather than creating punitive regional penalties, our current priority, supported by the Second Asean Haze-Free Roadmap 2023-2030, is to close implementation gaps, boost enforcement capacity and improve real-time monitoring across all member states."
The ministry said Malaysia was using diplomatic channels to push for swifter action following recent haze risks.
It said on Aug 21, Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Minister Datuk Seri Arthur Joseph Kurup had urged Asean members to scale up fire prevention measures, adding that Malaysia also held bilateral talks with Indonesia on Aug 24 to reinforce early suppression efforts during the El Nino season.
Recurring haze was also not attributable to a single factor, but resulted from a combination of land and forest management, peatland conditions, human activities, fire management and hot and dry weather, it said.
The ministry said Malaysia had also proposed science diplomacy as an approach to strengthen regional cooperation under the AATHP.
This would enable greater use of science and evidence to understand fire and haze risks, support decision-making and improve preventive and response measures.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Sarawak haze crisis: Kuching API hits 407, six areas in hazardous zone
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 1 — Six areas in Sarawak recorded Air Pollutant Index (API) readings at the hazardous level as of 8 am today, with the Serian District Police Headquarters recording the highest reading at 408.
According to data from the Air Pollutant Index Management System (APIMS) portal, the five other areas in Sarawak that recorded hazardous API readings were Kuching (407), Samarahan (372), Sri Aman (361), Sarikei (333) and Sibu (309).
Three areas in Sarawak recorded readings at the very unhealthy level – Mukah (234), Bintulu (232) and Samalaju (225).
Nine areas recorded unhealthy API readings, with the Miri Industrial Training Institute recording the highest reading at 187, followed by Miri (180), Kapit (178), Labuan (167) and Limbang (166).
Also recording unhealthy readings were Kimanis and Keningau in Sabah, both at 156, Tawau (132), and Johan Setia in Selangor (123).
Forty-eight areas nationwide were reported to have moderate API readings.
An API reading of zero to 50 indicates good air quality, 51 to 100 moderate, 101 to 200 unhealthy, 201 to 300 very unhealthy, and readings above 300 are classified as hazardous. — Bernama

Title: Dear Malaysia: Our shared beloved home
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 1 —
Selamat Hari Kebangsaan
and
Selamat Hari Malaysia
, my dear fellow Malaysians.
For the past five years, I have shared my thoughts with you around National Day.
Each year, I reflected on the many challenges facing our beloved nation; our economy, education, corruption, political reforms, climate change, artificial intelligence and the rapidly changing world around us.
These challenges remain relevant and important. This year, I would like to speak about something even more fundamental – who we are as a people.
I often ask myself a simple question. What do all Malaysians have in common?
Before we are Malays, Chinese, Indians, Ibans, Kadazans, Orang Asli or Eurasian and before we belong to different political parties or hold different opinions — who are we?
We are all sons and daughters of Malaysia. Many of us become husbands and wives. Many become mothers and fathers.
We celebrate when our children succeed. We lose sleep when they struggle. We worry when our parents grow old. We grieve when those we love leave us. We hope that the next generation will enjoy a better life than we did.
When we strip away everything else, we discover something beautiful and enlightening. We are far more alike than we are different.
I grew up in a small town called Pusing in Perak. My closest childhood friends were Malays, Chinese and Indians.
We played sports together. We swam in the old mining pools and rivers together. We often visited and slept over in one another’s homes.
I honestly cannot remember asking anyone what race they were before deciding whether they could be my friend.
Children have a remarkable gift. They see people before they see labels. Perhaps somewhere along the journey of adulthood, we lose a little of that wisdom.
Every child born into this world is a gift to humankind. None of us had the privilege to choose the colour of our skin and where we were born. Faith is indeed a deeply personal matter. None of us chose our first language and the family into which we entered this world.
Every one of us can decide, every single day, what kind of Malaysian we want to become. That choice has always been ours. And it will always be.
Whatever our faith may be, all religions teach us the same fundamental truth and wisdom, that every human life possesses dignity. Whatever our faith, surely none teaches us to despise another human being because of race or religion.
At Sunway, I always strive to ensure we are “colour-blind, passport-blind and religion-blind”.
As a nation of diverse cultures and creeds, our diversity is indeed a strength to be cherished.
We must deepen our resolve to build a country where all may live with dignity and a true sense of belonging.
Hatred is learnt. Respect can also be learnt. Division is cultivated. Unity can also be cultivated. The question before us is not whether Malaysia can become a more united nation.
The question is whether each of us is prepared to become a more generous Malaysian. Because nations do not become better by themselves. People do.
Throughout history, there have always been those who unite people. Unfortunately, there are also those who sought to divide us.
Division is easy. It takes little effort to convince one community to fear another.
It takes far greater courage to build trust. Oftentimes, there is a heavy price to pay for doing what is right and just.
We must remain steadfast in our convictions to uphold the ideals that bind us as a nation.
Every generation is eventually remembered by the bridges it built, or the walls it left behind. Our generation will be no different.
Sometimes I wonder how much further Malaysia might already have progressed if we had devoted the same energy to solving our common problems as we have spent fighting and arguing over our differences.
Imagine if we competed to build better schools instead of sharper slogans, if we invested more in educating our children than in insulting one another. Imagine if we became known not for the loudest voices, but for the wisest ideas on how to build a better nation.
On a global scale, imagine if America and China chose to work together as brothers and not rivals, the world would be a far better place for all humanity.
When I was a young boy, poverty shaped my life. It taught me that education is the most powerful pathway out of hardship and misery towards a life of dignity. That conviction never left me.
The success of my business career has given me the privilege to set up the Jeffrey Cheah Foundation to make quality education accessible to as many young Malaysians as possible, regardless of race and background.
This is why I transferred, in perpetuity, my entire equity in the Sunway Education Group (Sunway International Schools, Sunway Colleges and Sunway University) to the Jeffrey Cheah Foundation in a not-for-profit structure.
The foundation no longer belongs to me nor my family. It belongs to Malaysia for the benefit of present and future generations of Malaysians.
More than RM4 billion has been gifted and endowed in perpetuity through the foundation, with over RM1.05 billion in scholarships and grants awarded to date.
Every scholarship awarded is not simply another student entering college or university. It is a family lifted out of the vicious cycle of poverty and misery. A dream restored. A future rewritten. That, to me, is nation-building.
Yet governments alone cannot build a great nation. Businesses, schools, religious organisations and parents cannot do it alone.
Every citizen has a part to play. A better Malaysia is not something we inherit. It is something we build, together.
The world will not wait for us. Artificial Intelligence is transforming how we live, learn and work. Climate change is reshaping our future. Our neighbours and other countries around the world are investing heavily in innovation, education and human capital.
While the world races forward, Malaysia cannot afford to be left behind and be distracted by fear, suspicion and endless division. Our children deserve better than that. They deserve a nation confident enough to compete with the rest of the world.
Whether Malaysia remains competitive regionally or globally is really a question of how well prepared our next generation is for that competition.
Our duty as fathers, mothers and grandparents is to prepare our next generation to meet this very fierce, intensive and relentless competition.
In spite of all the challenges before us, I remain hopeful. Whenever I meet young Malaysians, I am encouraged by their curiosity, creativity, compassion and confidence.
Perhaps they will succeed where previous generations, including mine, have sometimes fallen short. Perhaps they will finally build the Malaysia we have always dreamed of. I sincerely believe they can and pray they will succeed.
Every one of us will leave this world one day. People are unlikely to remember which political party we supported. They will probably not remember the arguments we fought and debated on social media.
But they will remember whether we left Malaysia in a better state than we found it.
Kinder, fairer, more united, more stable and more hopeful. That, to me, is the true meaning of patriotism. Not merely loving our country for what it is today but loving it enough to help it become the Malaysia that we can all be proud of.
This is our home and shared inheritance. This is our responsibility and shared destiny.
Let us build bridges strong enough for the next generation to cross. Let us foster a more stable, just, inclusive and sustainable future for our beloved country.
Because the Malaysia we leave behind is the Malaysia our children will inherit.
Together, with conviction, let us build a nation worthy of them.
We are all in this together and may we all be blessed, always.
Selamat Hari Kebangsaan
.
Selamat Hari Malaysia
.
* Tan Sri Sir Dr Jeffrey Cheah KBE AO is a fellow Malaysian.

Title: Fatal LPT1 accident: Four dead in 11-vehicle crash near Kuantan
Article:
KUANTAN, Sept 1 — Four people were killed in an accident involving 11 vehicles at KM110 of the East Coast Expressway 1 (LPT1) from Lanchang towards Kuantan yesterday.
Pahang Fire and Rescue Department operations assistant director Mohd Salahuddin Isa said the department received an emergency call at 10.44 pm.
He said those killed were trapped in two vehicles. They comprised a man, a woman and a boy in one car and another male in a separate vehicle.
Firemen helped extricate all the victims before they were pronounced dead by Health Ministry personnel.
He said the crash also involved a bus, but all 30 passengers escaped unharmed. — Bernama

Title: Search for fisherman off Pulau Tenggol ends with no clues found
Article:
DUNGUN, Sept 1 — The search and rescue (SAR) operation for fisherman Sabrie Rusli, 32, who was feared missing after his boat capsized in the waters off Pulau Tenggol near here last Thursday, was called off yesterday after no clues or discoveries were detected.
Kemaman Maritime Zone Director Maritime Commander Abdul Halim Hamzah said the search operation for the fisherman covered an area of approximately 801.22 square nautical miles and was carried out systematically, taking into account weather conditions, sea states, currents, and the possibility of the victim drifting.
“Throughout the operation, various search methods were implemented, including surface searches, the use of sonar, diving operations, and a Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV) to help detect any clues or objects believed to be related to the victim.
“However, until the operation was called off, no clues or discoveries linking to the victim were successfully detected,” he said in a statement yesterday, adding that the decision to end the operation was made after all identified search sectors had been covered, and no new information was obtained to assist in locating the victim.
He stated that the Malaysian Maritime Enforcement Agency (MMEA) expressed its appreciation and thanks to all agencies, rescue teams, the maritime community, and parties involved directly or indirectly throughout the operation.
“Although the SAR operation has been called off, MMEA assets conducting routine patrols will continue to monitor the area in case there is any new information or discovery regarding the victim,” he said.
Previously, Bernama reported that Sabrie was believed missing after the boat he was riding in capsized in the waters off Pulau Tenggol at 5 pm last Thursday.
The incident is believed to have occurred while the victim, who was in a fiberglass boat, was on his way back after going out fishing at 9 am. — Bernama

Title: Malaysia Day address should bring further reforms for workers, small businesses, says Guan Eng
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 1 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim should use his Malaysia Day address on Sept 15 to announce further economic reforms to ease cost-of-living pressures and support small businesses, DAP MP for Bagan Lim Guan Eng said today.
In a statement, Lim welcomed several measures announced by Anwar in his National Day address on Aug 30, but said more could still be done to help wage earners and micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs).
“Anwar’s announcement that the annual sales threshold for exemption from mandatory e-Invoicing would be raised from RM1 million to RM3 million may disappoint those hoping for the threshold to be raised to RM5 million,” he said.
Lim said the higher threshold would nevertheless benefit about 1.1 million MSMEs by exempting them from mandatory e-Invoicing requirements.
He also welcomed the restoration of the Budi95 petrol subsidy quota to 300 litres a month and the setting of the BudiDiesel quota at 400 litres a month from today.
Other measures cited by Lim included an increase in the school maintenance allocation from RM1 billion to RM1.5 billion next year, an additional RM200 million for hawkers and small traders, and RM1 billion to improve digital capabilities in public healthcare.
He also pointed to free three-month subscriptions to artificial intelligence applications for 100,000 youths aged 18 to 30 who complete the required modules.
However, Lim said an additional RM1 billion for government microfinancing facilities, bringing the total allocation for 2026 to RM6 billion, remained insufficient for about 1.2 million MSMEs facing rising costs and price-cutting competition.
He renewed his call for a one-year interest moratorium on existing MSME loans and interest-free, collateral-free loans of up to RM50,000.
“The banking industry can help to bear the whole or part of the cost of the one year interest rate moratorium of existing loans and interest free new RM50,000 loans to MSMEs,” he said.
“The banking industry is probably the only business sector in Malaysia that recorded a 13.5 per cent rise or RM6.5 billion increase in profit before tax in 2025 to RM54.8 billion as compared to RM48.3 billion in 2024,” he added.
Lim also proposed abolishing the two per cent Employees Provident Fund contribution involving foreign workers, expanding and simplifying foreign worker recruitment, and reconsidering whether undocumented foreign workers already in Malaysia could be allowed to work legally.
He further called for a Special Taxpayers Tribunal to resolve disputes involving individuals and MSMEs and the Inland Revenue Board, as well as an increase in personal income tax relief by RM3,000 to RM12,000.
Several of the proposals had been raised by Lim earlier this year, including the MSME loan relief, foreign worker measures and the proposed taxpayers’ tribunal, while he had also previously called for the e-Invoicing exemption threshold to be raised to RM5 million.

Title: Fahmi hails behind-the-scenes heroes of National Day celebration
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 1 — Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil expressed his highest appreciation and gratitude to all parties who worked tirelessly to ensure the success of today’s 2026 National Day celebration.
He said that the appreciation was extended to everyone involved from the early stages of preparations until the conclusion of the celebration, including participants, security personnel, healthcare workers, media practitioners, volunteers and relevant agencies.
“A special thank you to all Malaysians who came to enliven Dataran Putrajaya, as well as the millions who watched the celebration from home.
“Your presence and spirit made this year’s celebration truly meaningful,” he said in a Facebook post yesterday.
Fahmi also described all those working behind the scenes as heroes who ensured the smooth running of the celebration.
“May the Malaysia we love continue to be blessed with prosperity, harmony and stability, and remain united in diversity. Happy National Day,” he said. — Bernama

Title: Bercham 10 fire: One hurt as major blaze damages nine factory lots in Ipoh
Article:
IPOH, Sept 1 —  A man suffered burns to his body in a fire that spread to nine factory lots in Persiaran Industri Bercham 10, Bercham here yesterday.
Perak Fire and Rescue Department asst operations director Sabarodzi Nor Ahmad said the man, 42, suffered burns to one per cent of his body and received first aid from emergency medical rescue services (EMRS) on the scene after a team of seven fire engines and 40 personnel responded to the fire after a call at 3.36 pm.
"The fire had started at a Class B plastics factory measuring 30 metres (m) by 13 m, which was 50 per cent burned, while other affected factories, Lot 10 and 11 suffered 20 per cent damage, Lots 12, 13 and 14 (70 per cent), Lots 16 and 18 (80 per cent), Lot 15 (10 per cent) and Lot 17 (60 per cent),” he said in a statement yesterday.
The fire was brought under control at 6.25 pm and firefighters were conducting overhaul work, inspections and putting out residual fires to ensure there were no more fire sources, he added. — Bernama

Title: Two killed, four hurt in boat crash near Mersing jetty
Article:
MERSING, Sept 1 — Two people died, while four others were injured in a two-boat collision near the Sungai Mersing estuary here last night.
The Fire and Rescue Department’s (JBPM) Operations Control Centre reported receiving an emergency call regarding the incident at 9:04 pm.
Following that, a Fire Rescue Tender and a Fire Response Vehicle (FRV) with a strength of nine personnel from the Mersing Fire and Rescue Station (BBP) were rushed to the Mersing Jetty.
“Upon the arrival of the Operation Team (PKO), it was confirmed that a collision had indeed occurred between two boats. Two victims were confirmed dead by medical personnel and handed over to the police for further action,” according to the statement.
Fire authorities reported that four other victims who sustained injuries are receiving treatment and the operation is still ongoing.
Meanwhile, Mersing District Police Chief Supt Abdul Razak Abdullah Sani confirmed the incident and said that the case is still under investigation, with a media statement to be issued shortly. — Bernama

Title: Not a ‘fast lane’: Miros tells Malaysian motorists to keep left, overtake right
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 1 — Think the right-most lane on a Malaysian highway is simply the “fast lane”?
The Malaysian Institute of Road Safety Research (Miros) has a simpler rule: keep left, move right to overtake, then return left when it is safe.
Director of the Road Safety Engineering and Environment Research Centre Rizati Hamidun said the left lane is generally meant for normal travelling and slower-moving vehicles, while the middle lane can be used for travelling and, where appropriate, overtaking slower vehicles in the left lane.
“The right-most lane is primarily for overtaking and should not be treated as a permanent cruising lane, even by motorists travelling at the maximum speed limit,” she said.
“Traffic should respect the dedicated function of each lane. The lane is there for a purpose, and motorists need to understand what that purpose is.
“The more correct concept is to keep left, move to the right to overtake, and once you have completed the manoeuvre, return to the left when it is safe,” she said.
This is consistent with Rule 4 of the Road Traffic Rules 1959, which requires slower vehicles to be kept as near as practicable to the left and driven in a manner that does not obstruct faster traffic.
What each highway lane is for
On a three-lane highway, motorists should generally use the left lane for normal travelling, particularly if they are driving slower or operating heavy vehicles.
The middle lane can be used by motorists travelling at moderate speeds and by vehicles overtaking slower traffic in the left lane.
The right-most lane is primarily for overtaking, meaning a motorist travelling at 110kph on a highway with a 110kph speed limit does not automatically have the right to remain there indefinitely.
Rizati said motorists should return to the left after overtaking once there is sufficient clearance and it is safe to do so.
“You need to make sure there is adequate clearance from the vehicle that you have overtaken and that there is a sufficient gap in the lane you want to move into.
“Once you have that clearance, you should move back as soon as it is reasonably practical and safe to do so,” she said.
What if the driver ahead refuses to move?
A motorist approaching a slower vehicle in the right-most lane should first maintain a safe following distance rather than tailgate, while giving the driver ahead sufficient time and space to assess the traffic and move left safely.
Rizati said motorists should not respond to a vehicle that refuses to move by attempting a dangerous manoeuvre.
“If the front vehicle does not move aside, we cannot attempt a dangerous overtaking manoeuvre or overtake on the left simply out of impatience.
“We have to wait for a safe, lawful opportunity to overtake and give the vehicle in front enough time and space to move safely,” she said.
Can you flash your headlights?
Briefly flashing the headlights can be used to communicate an intention to overtake, but Rizati said it should not become an aggressive demand for another driver to move.
“One or two flashes are enough to give a signal that you want to overtake. After that, you have to wait for the vehicle ahead to move to the left in a safe condition,” she said.
Repeated flashing or tailgating could create tension and encourage unsafe driving, while a motorist travelling above the speed limit cannot expect another driver to immediately move aside simply because they want to travel faster.
What about the right indicator?
Using the right turn signal simply to tell a vehicle ahead to move aside is not recommended because indicators are intended to communicate an intention to turn or change lanes.
For example, a motorist in the middle lane intending to move into the right lane should activate the right indicator before making the lane change.
A driver already in the right-most lane, however, should not use the right indicator merely as a “move over” signal because there is no lane to the right.
“The right signal has a clear traffic-management purpose. It communicates an intention to move to the right or to turn right.
“If you are already in the right-most lane and put on your right signal simply to tell the vehicle ahead that you want to overtake, that can be misleading because there is no lane to your right,” she said.
Can you overtake on the left?
Miros advises motorists not to use the left lane simply to get around a vehicle occupying the right lane.
Rizati said a motorist could move into the left lane to continue travelling there, but should not use it as an overtaking manoeuvre before cutting back into the right lane.
“You can join the left lane and continue travelling there. The left lane should not be used to overtake a vehicle and then cut back to the right,” she said.
The distinction matters when a seemingly clear gap appears on the left while a vehicle ahead is occupying the right lane, as motorists should instead maintain a safe distance and wait for a lawful opportunity to overtake.
What does the law say about lane hogging?
Rule 4 of the Road Traffic Rules 1959 requires vehicles travelling at slow speeds to be driven as close as possible to the left and in a manner that does not obstruct faster vehicles.
Rule 4A specifically prohibits drivers of goods vehicles and public service vehicles from continuously using the extreme right lane on any road or highway, except when overtaking a vehicle ahead.
Rule 5 provides that motorists should overtake traffic travelling in the same direction from the right, subject to specified exceptions.
“Actually those travelling on the right lane all the time are committing an offence; it’s hogging the right lane. Meaning they’re maintaining (their vehicle) in the right lane, monopolising the lane and not letting others pass. It can also cause congestion because when a vehicle stays in the right lane without overtaking, it affects the movement of other vehicles behind it,” said Rizati.
“You can’t stay in the right lane too long. If you face this situation do not overtake on the left; that’s not allowed as well. Go back to the left lane and find a safe distance to move back to the right if you need to,” she said.
Lane hogging and speeding are separate issues: the former concerns failure to use the appropriate lane, while the latter involves driving above the legal speed limit.
So where do 60, 80 and 100kph come in?
Miros is currently conducting a minimum-speed advisory proof-of-concept initiative on selected sections of the PLUS Highway and South Klang Valley Expressway (SKVE), with motorists advised to maintain minimum speeds of 60kph in the left lane, 80kph in the middle lane and 100kph in the right lane where conditions permit.
The figures are advisories under the ongoing trial and are not intended to require motorists to maintain those speeds when doing so would be unsafe, such as during heavy rain or congestion.
Rizati said the initiative is intended partly to address large variations in vehicle speeds and poor lane discipline, as motorists previously had a maximum speed limit but no corresponding minimum-speed reference for different lanes.
“We would like to test whether 60 is suitable for this lane, whether 80 is suitable for this lane and whether 100 is suitable for this lane.
“We also want to minimise speed variation because previously we only had a maximum speed limit. Everyone could drive at their own favourable speed, and the variation could become very large,” she said.
The initiative is also intended to improve traffic flow and safety while reducing aggressive overtaking from the left.
Rizati said feedback so far had been generally positive, although the trial remains ongoing and Miros has yet to draw final conclusions.
“This is only a trial. So far, it is progressing and people are responding to it. We have received a lot of positive feedback.
“We still have August, September and until the end of October, so there is quite a long way to go. We cannot judge it yet,” she said.
The simple rule
For motorists, Miros’ message is straightforward: keep left, use the right lane to overtake, give other drivers time and space to move over, and return left once the manoeuvre is safely completed.
The right-most lane may commonly be called the “fast lane”, but travelling at the maximum speed limit does not make it a permanent cruising lane.
Likewise, being stuck behind a slower vehicle is not a licence to tailgate, repeatedly flash the headlights or attempt an unsafe manoeuvre.
Good lane discipline ultimately comes down to recognising that every lane has a purpose.
Know your highway lanes
Left: Normal travelling and slower-moving or heavy vehicles; 60kph minimum-speed advisory under the current trial.
Middle: Normal travelling and appropriate overtaking of slower traffic; 80kph minimum-speed advisory under the current trial.
Right: Primarily for overtaking; 100kph minimum-speed advisory under the current trial, where conditions permit.
Remember: The 60/80/100kph figures are minimum-speed advisories under the current proof-of-concept trial, not blanket instructions to maintain those speeds regardless of weather, traffic or road conditions.
If you’re behind someone in the right lane
Keep a safe following distance.
Give the vehicle ahead time and space to move over.
One or two brief headlight flashes can signal that you want to overtake.
Do not repeatedly flash, tailgate or harass the driver.
Do not use the right indicator simply to say “move over”.
Do not use the left lane to undertake and then cut back into the right lane.
Once you have overtaken, return left when it is safe.

Title: Budi Madani: Restored RON95 quota, higher diesel allocation bring relief to motorists, traders
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 31 — The government’s decision to restore the assistance quota under the Budi Madani programme for RON95 petrol and increase the diesel quota has been well received by various layers of society and traders, considering it a timely step in alleviating the burden of living costs.
The announcement was made by Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim during the 2026 National Day “Amanat Perdana” address at the Putrajaya International Convention Centre (PICC) yesterday.
In the address, he announced that the basic eligibility quota for RON95 petrol subsidies would be increased from 200 litres to 300 litres, while the Budi Diesel quota would be raised from 300 litres to 400 litres, effective today.
On average, beneficiaries stated that the return of the quota provided relief, especially in terms of monthly finances, and allowed expenses to be allocated to other basic needs.
Private sector worker, Furzani Ahmad, 24, said that the return of this quota contributed tremendously towards his commute to work.
For me, with this Budi 95, I can save a little on my monthly expenses. Almost every day, the distance I have to travel is almost 30 kilometres (km), so 300 litres is enough for a month, and sometimes there could even be surplus,” he said when met by Bernama.
Also sharing the same view, Darwisy Khairudin, 23, was happy with the government’s decision to restore the Budi 95 quota.
“The distance from my workplace to my home is only about 20 km to 25 km, but sometimes I have outside assignments, so I have to calculate whether the fuel quota is enough or not. Therefore, it’s really good that the government has reinstated this quota,” Darwisy said.
Meanwhile, fruit stall operator Abdul Manan, 63, who uses a diesel vehicle to transport his supplies, described the increase in the Budi Diesel quota as helping to stabilise his daily operating costs.
He said that the return of the quota reduces the burden of logistics expenses, thereby allowing him to maintain reasonable fruit prices for customers.
“Sometimes we take stocks from far away, so the petrol consumption is definitely high. Therefore the increase in the diesel quota at least provides relief to our working capital so that the selling price does not need to be raised,” he said.
The Budi Madani programme is a government initiative to ensure that fuel subsidies are distributed in a targeted manner. — Bernama

Title: College student dies after fall from Setapak condominium
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 31 — An 18-year-old college student died after falling from the 22nd floor of a condominium in Setapak here this morning.
Free Malaysia Today reported that Wangsa Maju police chief Annas Sulaiman said police were alerted at about 8.50am after a security guard found the student’s body at Residensi Teratai on Jalan Langkawi.
The victim, a first-semester student at Universiti Geomatika Malaysia, had returned to the university-provided condominium unit at about 7.07am, according to CCTV footage reviewed by police.
Annas said the footage showed the student subsequently falling from a corridor on the 22nd floor to the sixth floor.
“The victim was confirmed dead at the scene. The case has been classified as sudden death and further investigations are being held to complete the probe,” he said in a statement.
